The '''visual arts of Sudan''' encompass the historical and contemporary production of objects made by the inhabitants of today's [[Republic of the Sudan]] and specific to their respective cultures. This encompasses objects from cultural traditions of the region in North-East Africa [[History of Sudan|historically referred to as the Sudan]], including the southern regions that became independent as [[South Sudan]] in 2011.

Throughout its history, Sudan has been a crossroads between [[North Africa]], [[Egypt]], [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] cultures, parts of [[West Africa]] and the [[Red Sea]] coast in the east of the country. Before the 20th century, these cultural traditions were influenced by indigenous African, [[Pharaoh|Pharaonic]], [[Greco-Roman world|Greco-Roman]], [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] and [[Arab culture|Arabic]] cultures that have brought about a large diversity of cultural expressions, often specific to the ethnic or social group that produced and used them.<ref group="note">In the article on the cultural life in Sudan, the [[Encyclopædia Britannica]] writes: "The key to an understanding of contemporary Sudanese culture is diversity. Each major ethnic group and historical region has its own special forms of cultural expression. (...) Because of Sudan's great cultural diversity, it is difficult to classify the traditional cultures of the various peoples. Sudan's traditional societies have diverse linguistic, ethnic, social, cultural, and religious characteristics. And, although improved communications, increased social and economic mobility, and the spread of a money economy have led to a general loosening of the social ties, customs, relationships, and modes of organization in traditional cultures, much from the past still remains intact." {{Cite web|title=Sudan – Cultural life|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Sudan|access-date=28 April 2021|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|language=en}}</ref> As expressions of the [[material culture]] of a society, [[applied arts]] and [[handicraft]]s are included with the fine arts in this history of the arts in Sudan.

Starting in the early 19th century, the establishment of first the [[Turkish Sudan|Turkish-Egyptian]] and later the [[Anglo-Egyptian Sudan|Anglo-Egyptian]] rule, characterised by foreign military and political domination, ushered in the gradual evolution of a modern [[nation state]] with new cultural influences on the lifestyles and material culture of the Sudanese.

After [[Republic of the Sudan (1956–1969)|independence in 1956]], Sudanese graduates of the colonial education system took over leading positions in the new state and thus contributed to the emergence of urban culture and [[modern art]]. These cultural developments became most visible from the 1950s to the 1980s, a period that was later called "''The Making of the Modern Art Movement in Sudan''".

In the 21st century, visual artistic developments in the country have been characterised by digital forms of communication, including [[Audiovisual|audio-visual]] art spread and received through satellite television, [[online media]] as well as images and films shared through social media.<ref group=note>This is mainly true for people with access to electronic devices, which still excludes large sections of Sudanese society, especially in rural areas. These changes in communication, style of life and general attitudes are of growing importance.</ref> During the [[Sudanese Revolution]] of 2018 and 2019, young artists contributed to the protests and morale of the popular movement, creating wall paintings, graffiti, cartoons, photographs or video messages.

{{Culture of Singapore sidebar}}{{History of art sidebar}}The '''visual art of Singapore''', or '''Singaporean art''', refers to all forms of [[Visual arts|visual art]] in or associated with [[Singapore]] throughout its history and towards the present-day. The history of Singaporean art includes the indigenous artistic traditions of the [[Malay Archipelago]] and the diverse visual practices of itinerant artists and migrants from [[China]], the [[Indian subcontinent]], and [[Europe]].<ref name=":62">{{Cite book |last=Susanto |first=Melinda |title=Siapa Nama Kamu? Art in Singapore Since the 19th Century |publisher=National Gallery Singapore |year=2015 |isbn=978-981-14-0557-0 |location=Singapore |pages=30–41 |chapter=Tropical Tapestry}}</ref>

Singaporean art includes the sculptural, [[Textile arts|textile]], and [[Decorative arts|decorative art]] traditions of the [[Malay world]]; [[portrait]]ure, [[Landscape painting|landscapes]], [[sculpture]], [[printmaking]], and [[natural history]] drawings from the country's British colonial period; along with [[Nanyang Style|Nanyang style]] paintings, [[Social realism|social realist art]], [[abstract art]], and [[photography]] practices emerging in the post-war period.<ref name=":62"/> Today, it includes the [[contemporary art]] practices of post-independence Singapore, such as [[performance art]], [[conceptual art]], [[installation art]], [[video art]], [[sound art]], and [[new media art]].<ref name=":452">{{Cite book |last=Toh |first=Charmaine |title=Siapa Nama Kamu? Art in Singapore Since the 19th Century |date=2015 |publisher=National Gallery Singapore |isbn=978-981-09-7384-1 |editor-last=Low |editor-first=Sze Wee |page=92 |chapter=Shifting Grounds}}</ref>

The emergence of [[Modern art|modern]] Singaporean art, or more specifically, "the emergence of self-aware artistic expression"<ref name=":62" /> is often tied to the rise of art associations, art schools, and exhibitions in the 20th century, though this has since been expanded to include earlier forms of visual representation, such as from Singapore's pre-colonial periods.<ref name=":42">{{Cite book |title=Siapa Nama Kamu? Art in Singapore since the 19th Century |publisher=National Gallery Singapore |year=2015 |isbn=978-981-09-7352-0 |editor-last=Low |editor-first=Sze Wee |location=Singapore |pages=8–29 |chapter=Some Introductory Remarks}}</ref><ref name=":022">{{Cite web |date=12 October 2016 |title=T.K. Sabapathy |url=https://www.esplanade.com/offstage/arts/t-k-sabapathy |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227025531/https://www.esplanade.com/offstage/arts/t-k-sabapathy |archive-date=27 February 2021 |access-date=27 February 2021 |website=Esplanade Offstage}}</ref>

Presently, the [[contemporary art]] of Singapore also circulates internationally through art [[biennale]]s and other major international exhibitions. Contemporary art in Singapore tends to examine themes of "hyper-modernity and the built environment; alienation and changing social mores; [[Postcolonialism|post-colonial]] identities and [[multiculturalism]]."<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Teh |first=David |date=2017 |title=Insular Visions: notes on video art in Singapore |url=https://www.academia.edu/29987712 |journal=The Japan Foundation Asia Center Art Studies |volume=3 |via=Academia.org |access-date=2021-05-17 |archive-date=2023-01-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230108202307/https://www.academia.edu/29987712 |url-status=live }}</ref> Across these tendencies, "the exploration of [[Performance art|performance]] and the performative body" is a common running thread.<ref name=":12" /> Singapore carries a notable history of [[performance art]], with the government historically having enacted a no-funding rule for that specific art form from 1994 to 2003, following a controversial performance artwork at the [[5th Passage]] art space.<ref name=":23">{{Cite book |last=Lee |first=Weng Choy |url=https://www.academia.edu/1330638 |title=Looking at Culture |date=1996 |publisher=Artres Design & Communications |isbn=981-00-6714-3 |editor-last=Krishnan |editor-first=S.K. Sanjay |location=Singapore |chapter=Chronology of a Controversy |editor-last2=Lee |editor-first2=Weng Choy |editor-last3=Perera |editor-first3=Leon |editor-last4=Yap |editor-first4=Jimmy |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200608200204/https://www.academia.edu/1330638/Chronology_of_a_Controversy |archive-date=8 June 2020}}</ref><ref name=":52">{{Cite journal |last=Lingham |first=Susie |date=November 2011 |title=Art and Censorship in Singapore: Catch 22? |url=http://artasiapacific.com/Magazine/76/ArtAndCensorshipInSingaporeCatch22  |journal=ArtAsiaPacific |issue=76 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140915073253/http://artasiapacific.com/Magazine/76/ArtAndCensorshipInSingaporeCatch22 |archive-date=15 September 2014 |access-date=8 June 2020}}</ref>

'''Organotechnetium chemistry''' is the science of describing the physical properties, synthesis, and reactions of '''organotechnetium compounds''', which are [[organometallic compound]]s containing [[carbon]]-to-[[technetium]] [[chemical bonds]]. The most common organotechnetium compounds are [[coordination complexes]] used as [[radiopharmaceutical]] imaging agents.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Kowalsky RJ | title = Technetium Radiopharmaceutical Chemistry. | publisher = The University of New Mexico. Health Sciences Center, College of Pharmacy | date = 2006 | volume = 12 | issue = 3 | pages = 1–77 | url = https://pharmacyce.unm.edu/nuclear_program/freelessonfiles/vol12lesson3.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ritter SK | title = Good reasons to study technetium chemistry | journal = Chemical & Engineering News | date = April 2017 |  volume = 95 | issue = 15 |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i15/reasons-study-technetium-chemistry.html|access-date=2021-06-12 }}</ref>

In general, organotechnetium compounds are not typically used in [[chemical reaction]]s or [[catalysis]] due to their [[radioactivity]]. Research on technetium chemistry is often done in conjunction with [[rhenium]] as a [[Isoelectronicity|isoelectronic]] non-radioactive alternative to technetium.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jürgens|first1=Sophie|last2=Herrmann|first2=Wolfgang A.|last3=Kühn|first3=Fritz E.|date=February 2014|title=Rhenium and technetium based radiopharmaceuticals: Development and recent advances|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022328X13005494|journal=Journal of Organometallic Chemistry|language=en|volume=751|pages=83–89|doi=10.1016/j.jorganchem.2013.07.042|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The '''''Journal of Geography''''' is an American academic journal published by Taylor & Francis on behalf of the [[National Council for Geographic Education]] (NCGE).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ncge.org/teacher-resources/publications/the-journal-of-geography/|title=The Journal of Geography – National Council for Geographic Education}}</ref> The journal "provides a forum to present innovative approaches to geography research, teaching, and learning. The Journal publishes original studies, critical reviews, case insights, methods, and evaluations of books."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/toc/rjog20/current|title=Journal of Geography|newspaper=Taylor & Francis}}</ref>

{{as of|2026}}, the Editor-in-chief is Injeong Jo of Texas State University, USA <ref>[https://www.tandfonline.com/action/journalInformation?show=editorialBoard&journalCode=rjog20 Journal web site about page]</ref> The journal has a 5-year Impact Factor of 2.2 as of 2024 <ref><Journal metrics [https://www.tandfonline.com/action/journalInformation?show=journalMetrics&journalCode=rjog20]</ref>

''Journal of Geography'' was first published in 1902 by the American Geographical Society (AGS). The journal was gifted by AGS to the National Council of Geography Teachers (later renamed National Council for Geographic Education) in 1915. The fifteenth volume of the journal (for 1916-17), was the first produced under the guidance of NCGE and Editor Ray Hughes Whitbeck of the University of Wisconsin with a new coverline:  "A Monthly Magazine Devoted to the Interests of Teachers of Geography in Elementary, Secondary, and Normal Schools."<ref>https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00221341608986362</ref>

The '''British Physics Olympiad''' ('''BPhO''') is a series of ten [[competition]]s in the study of [[physics]] for students in years 11–13 in the [[United Kingdom]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.stem.org.uk/resources/elibrary/resource/420294/british-physics-olympiad | title=British Physics Olympiad | website=www.stem.org.uk | publisher=STEM Learning | location=UK | accessdate=8 October 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://stepmaths.co.uk/physics-olympiad/ | title=British Physics Olympiad | website=stepmaths.co.uk | publisher=The Oxbridge Formula | location=UK | accessdate=8 October 2021 }}</ref>

On a day-to-day basis, the BPhO is run by five committee members as well as a large team of volunteer physics teachers and academics from across the UK.<ref name="about">{{Cite web | url=https://www.bpho.org.uk/about | title=About Us | publisher=British Physics Olympiad | location=UK | accessdate=8 October 2021 | archive-date=14 November 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211114212814/https://www.bpho.org.uk/about | url-status=dead }}</ref> The BPhO's administrative office is based in the [[Denys Wilkinson Building]] of the [[Department of Physics, University of Oxford|Department of Physics]]<ref name="about" /> at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.oxforduniversitystores.co.uk/product-catalogue/physics/british-physics-olympiad-competitions | title=British Physics Olympiad Competitions | website=www.oxforduniversitystores.co.uk | publisher=[[University of Oxford]] | location=UK | accessdate=8 October 2021 | archive-date=16 January 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220116200152/https://www.oxforduniversitystores.co.uk/product-catalogue/physics/british-physics-olympiad-competitions | url-status=dead }}</ref> The BPhO is a [[charitable trust]].

{{Short description|Visual art forms associated with Manichaeism}}
[[File:Seal_of_Mani_(cleaned_up)._Seal_with_figure_of_Mani,_possibly_3rd_century_CE,_possibly_Irak._Cabinet_des_Médailles,_Paris.jpg|thumb|The [[Sealstone of Mani|seal of Mani]], the oldest known Manichaean art]]
[[Manichaeism]] has a rich tradition of visual art, starting with [[Mani (prophet)|Mani]] himself writing [[Arzhang|the Book of Pictures]].<ref name="Arnold 1924 23–24">{{cite book |last= Arnold |first= Thomas |date= 1924 |title= Survivals of Sasanian and Manichaean Art in Persian painting |location= Oxford |publisher= Clarendon Press |pages= 23–24 }}</ref>

One of Mani's primary beliefs was that the [[arts]] (namely [[painting]], [[calligraphy]], and [[music]]) were of the same esteem as the [[Holy Spirit|divine spirit]] ([[Middle Persian]]: ''Mihryazd''), believing that the creation of art was comparable to [[Manichaeism#Cosmogony|god's creation of living forms]], and therefore the experience of art was more of a divine act than any other in the [[Universe|material world]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Klimkeit |first=Hans-Joachim |date=1982 |title=Manichaean Art And Calligraphy |location=New York |publisher=Brill |page= 60 |isbn=9004064788 }}</ref> Throughout the [[Manichaeism#History|history of Manichaeism]], didactic books of paintings were used to illustrate the religion's teachings and beliefs. From the beginning, the prophet Mani envisioned his religion (which included the teachings of [[Zarathustra]], [[Buddha]], and [[Christ]]) as a universal and therefore “[[Transculturalism|transcultural]]” entity, leading to its [[Manichaeism#Spread|vast spread from Europe to Asia]]. The Manichaean mission employed multifaceted means of communication (including oral, textual, and pictorial) so the beliefs may adapt to the variety of cultures it entered. These picture books covered the [[Manichaeism#Teachings and beliefs|primary themes of Manichaeism]], such as its [[Dualistic cosmology|dualism of light and darkness]], maps of a religious universe, the [[Sermon on Mani's Teaching of Salvation|process of human salvation]], as well as various [[Manichaeism#Cosmogony|Manichaean prophets and deities]], and were considered principal pieces of the Manichaean canon.<ref name="Gulácsi">{{cite journal |url=https://heiup.uni-heidelberg.de/journals/index.php/transcultural/article/view/6173/2966#_edn1 |title=Searching for Mani's Picture Book in Textual and Pictorial Sources |last=Gulácsi |first=Zsuzsanna |date=June 29, 2011 |journal=Transcultural Studies |volume=1 |issue=2011 |doi=10.11588/ts.2011.1.6173 |access-date=December 9, 2019 }}</ref>

On the subject of Mani's original paintings, [[Zsuzsanna Gulácsi|Dr. Zsuzsanna Gulácsi]] notes that the “paintings were created first in mid-third century Mesopotamia with direct involvement from Mani ... and were later preserved by being copied and adapted to a wide variety of artistic and cultural norms, as the religion spread across the Asian continent.”<ref name="Mani's-Pictures">{{cite book |last=Gulácsi |first=Zsuzsanna |date=2015 |title=Mani's Pictures: The Didactic Images of the Manichaeans from Sasanian Mesopotamia to Uygur Central Asia and Tang-Ming China |series="Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies" series |volume=90 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rUUpCwAAQBAJ&q=Manichaean+Diagram+of+the+Universe&pg=PA440 |location=Leiden |publisher=Brill Publishers |page=440 |isbn=9789004308947 }}</ref> Gulácsi points to the [[Yuan dynasty|Yuan]]-era silk paintings ''[[Manichaean Diagram of the Universe]]'' and ''[[Sermon on Mani's Teaching of Salvation]]'' as examples of [[sinicized]] variations of Mani's tradition of using a ''Book of Pictures'' as a method of teaching, specifically providing insight into the cosmology of the era's [[Chinese Manichaeism]].<ref name="Mani's-Pictures"/> After the discovery of fragmentary pieces of [[Uyghur people|Uyghur]]-[[Manichaeism|Manichean]] art<ref>Manichaean Art in Berlin Collections, "Corpus Fontium Manichaeorum : Series Archaeologica et Iconographica" (vol. 1). Turnhout: Brepols Publishers, 2001 (The book translated into Persian by [https://independent.academia.edu/6So0Mi9 Sonia Mirzaie], Tehran: [[Iranian Academy of Arts]], 2023 </ref> in the ruins of [[Turfan]], [[Western Regions]], scholars began turning to the newly uncovered remains of Manichaean book art in order to assess through the fragments what could resemble the original style of the ''Arzhang''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Klimkeit |first=Hans-Joachim |date=1982 |title=Manichaean Art And Calligraphy |location=New York |publisher=Brill |page= 231 |isbn=9004064788 }}</ref>

{{Culture of Uzbekistan}}{{Islamic culture}}
'''Uzbek literature''' refers to the literature produced and developed in the [[Uzbekistan|Republic of Uzbekistan]], as well as to literary works contributed by the Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan people of [[Central Asia]]. Influenced by  [[Russian literature|Russian]] and [[Turkish literature]], Uzbek is predominantly written in  [[Uzbek language|the Uzbek language]] with its roots in [[Chagatai language]], one of the widely accessible languages in the region from 14th to 20th century. In Uzbek literature, Chagatai plays an important role as a [[reference]]   point.

The history of Uzbek literature links ancient and modern Uzbekistan. Before the [[History of Uzbekistan|founding of Uzbekistan]], [[Soviet Central Asia|preceding colonies]] and the [[Russian conquest of Central Asia]] had significantly impacted Uzbek literature and continued to mark its presence until the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|Soviet Union was dissolved in 1991]]. Central [[Asian literature]], including Uzbek is thus linked to Turkish and Russian literature. However, much of Uzbek literature witnessed significant development in modern era due to its pre-existence in [[Uzbeks]].

Uzbek [[writing system]] observed significant changes by its native writers who switched from [[Turkic script]] to [[Arabic script|Arabic]] that originally began in the 10th century until the 12th century. This development adopted [[language reform]]s from [[Arabic literature]]. [[Yūsuf Balasaguni]], [[Mahmud al-Kashgari]], and [[Ahmad Yugnaki]] were among the leading writers of that time who flourished Uzbek literature by adopting language reforms. [[Ahmad Yasawi]] was also one of the other writers who introduced new genre in Uzbek literature. Yesevi's poetry collection ''Divan-i hikmet'' (Book of Wisdom) is composed of various dialects, such as Arabic and Persian, which features Turkic [[Metre (poetry)|metre]].

In the later years, Uzbek literature emerged in the Chagatai language between the 13th and 14th centuries. One of poets of that time was Khwārizmī who wrote ''Muhabbatnamah'' (Love Letters) that was preserved in the region and serves as a historical reference for [[Literary modernism|modern literature]].<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica">{{cite web | title=Uzbek literature | website=Encyclopedia Britannica | url=https://www.britannica.com/art/Uzbek-literature | access-date=2021-12-11}}</ref>

'''''The Power of Geography: Ten Maps that Reveal the Future of Our World''''' is a book on [[geopolitics]] by the British author and journalist [[Tim Marshall (journalist)|Tim Marshall]]. It was published by Elliott & Thompson in 2021 and is the sequel to his 2015 book ''[[Prisoners of Geography]]''.

In [[biology]], '''mimesis''' (from [[ancient Greek]] μίμησις ''mímēsis'', "imitation")<ref>[[Wilhelm Pape|Pape, Wilhelm]]; Sengebusch, Max (ed.): ''[http://images.zeno.org/Pape-1880/K/big/Pape-1880----02-0186.png Handwörterbuch der griechischen Sprache]'', volume 3, edition 6. Vieweg & Sohn, Braunschweig 1914.</ref> is a form of [[crypsis]] where living creatures mimic the form, colour and posture of their surroundings to avoid being noticed by predators depending on sight.<ref>Remane, Adolf; Storch, Volker; Welsch, Ulrich: ''Kurzes Lehrbuch der Zoologie'', volume 6, Gustav Fischer Verlag, Stuttgart 1989, {{ISBN|3-437-20436-X}}, p. 352.</ref> One view is that mimesis, being a form of crypsis, differs from [[mimicry]], but in [[English language|English]], mimesis is often counted as one of several forms of mimicry.<ref name="schaefer">Schaefer, Matthias: ''Wörterbuch der Ökologie'', volume 4, Spektrum Akademischer Verlag, Heidelberg, Berlin 2005. {{ISBN|3-8274-0167-4}}.</ref>

The '''Chinese semiconductor industry''', including [[integrated circuit]] design and manufacturing, forms a major part of mainland China's [[Electric power|electric technology]] industry.

China's semiconductor industry consists of a wide variety of companies, from [[integrated device manufacturer]]s to [[Semiconductor fabrication plant|pure-play foundries]], [[fabless semiconductor company|fabless semiconductor companies]] and OSAT companies. [[Integrated device manufacturer]]s (IDMs) design and manufacture integrated circuits. [[Semiconductor fabrication plant|Pure-play foundries]] only manufacture devices for other companies, without designing them, while [[fabless semiconductor company|fabless semiconductor companies]] only design devices. Examples of Chinese IDMs are [[YMTC]] and [[Changxin Memory Technologies|CXMT]]; examples of Chinese pure-play foundries are [[Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation|SMIC]], [[Hua Hong Semiconductor]] and [[Wingtech]]; examples of Chinese fabless companies are [[Zhaoxin]], [[HiSilicon]], [[Loongson]] and [[UNISOC]]; and examples of Chinese OSAT companies are [[JCET (company)|JCET]], [[Huatian Technology]] and [[Tongfu Microelectronics]].

'''Zimbabwean literature''' is literature produced by authors from Zimbabwe or in the [[Zimbabwean Diaspora]]. The tradition of literature starts with a long oral tradition, was influenced heavily by western literature that influenced multiple countries in the same region such as Malawi and Zambia whereby these three countries have very similar languages and a lot of words seem to be quite similar only that the tones or infliction or pronunciation is different because during colonial rule most slaves would run away, and acts as a form of protest to the government.<ref name=Convo/><ref>{{cite news|title=In Zimbabwe, literature is protest|url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/opinion/opinion/1999815/in-zimbabwe-literature-is-protest|date=10 October 2020|first=Beavan|last=Tapureta|website=[[Bangkok Post]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Literature and crisis in Zimbabwe|first=Ranka|last=Primorac|url=https://theguardian.com/books/booksblog/2008/apr/22/literatureandcrisisinzimba|date=22 April 2008|website=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref>

Prominent Zimbabwean writers include [[Doris Lessing]],  [[Dambudzo Marechera]],<ref>{{cite book|title=Reincarnating Marechera: Notes On a Speculative Archive|first=Tinashe|last=Mushakavanhu|author-link=Tinashe Mushakavanhu|date=2020|series=2020 Pamphlet Series|isbn=978-1-946433-60-2|publisher=Inpress Books}}</ref> [[NoViolet Bulawayo]],<ref name=Convo>{{cite web|url=https://theconversation.com/noviolet-bulawayos-new-novel-is-an-instant-zimbabwean-classic-185783|title=NoViolet Bulawayo's new novel is an instant Zimbabwean classic|first=Tinashe|last=Mushakavanhu|location=[[University of Oxford]]|date=27 July 2022|website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]|access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref> [[Chenjerai Hove]], [[Yvonne Vera]], [[Stanlake Samkange]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|chapter=Stanlake Samkange|year=2005|first=Ranka|last=Primorac|location=[[University of Southampton]]|editor1=[[John Thieme]]|title=The Literary Encyclopedia|volume=7.2.3.03|series=South Africa and other Southern Writing and Culture|editor2=[[Helen Rachel Cousins]]|editor3=[[David Firth (actor)|David Firth]]|publisher=The Literary Dictionary Company Limited}}</ref> and [[Tsitsi Dangarembga]].<ref name="Zimbabwe, she wrote">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2023/jul/28/zimbabwe-she-wrote-the-women-telling-their-countrys-story-for-a-new-era|title=Zimbabwe, she wrote: the women telling their country’s story for a new era|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|first=Tawanda|last=Mudzonga|date=28 July 2023}}</ref>

'''Guatemalan art''' refers to all forms of visual art associated with a Guatemalan national identity either because they are created within [[Guatemala]], for [[Guatemalans]], or by Guatemalans.  The [[visual arts]] in Guatemala consist largely of [[weaving]], [[mural]]ism, [[painting]], [[architecture]], and the [[performing arts]].  Most analysis of Guatemalan and Indigenous artwork focuses on the artform of weaving, but contemporary Guatemalan visual art largely consists of painting, muralism, and more that can convey modern social values as well as ancestral indigenous history.<ref name="Jurosz-2014">{{Cite journal |last=Jurosz |first=Gabriela |date=2014 |title=Anthropology of Art. Indigenous Concepts in Contemporary Art in Guatemala |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.5771/0257-9774-2014-1-206 |journal=Anthropos |volume=109 |issue=1 |pages=206–217 |doi=10.5771/0257-9774-2014-1-206 |issn=0257-9774|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  Historically, art in Guatemala has combined the mythological heritage of the [[Maya peoples|Indigenous Maya]] people with the country's politics.<ref name="Jurosz-2014" />  Beyond Guatemala, Guatemalan Indigenous artwork is also sometimes referred to as "art naïf," "primitivism," 'traditional art," "Maya art," and "costumbrismo".<ref name="Jurosz-2014" />

[[Traffic light]]s are signalling devices positioned at [[Intersection (road)|road intersections]], [[pedestrian crossing]]s, and other locations to control flows of traffic. The '''history of traffic lights''' is associated with the [[History of the automobile|historic growth of the automobile]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=McShane |first1=Clay |date=March 1999 |title=The Origins and Globalization of Traffic Control Signals |url=https://sites.tufts.edu/carscultureplace2010/files/2010/09/McShane-traffic-signals-1999.pdf |journal=Journal of Urban History |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=379–404 |doi=10.1177/009614429902500304 |s2cid=110125733 |access-date=27 October 2019}}</ref>[[File:White Horse Tavern NYWTS.jpg|thumb|An early two-light traffic signal by [[White Horse Tavern (New York City)|White Horse Tavern]] in [[Hudson Street (Manhattan)|Hudson Street]], [[New York City|New York]], 1961]]
Traffic lights were first introduced in December 1868 in [[London]] to assist police officers controlling traffic.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Matt |date=16 May 2023 |title=Here's What The World's First Traffic Lights, In Westminster, Looked Like |url=https://londonist.com/london/history/here-s-what-the-world-s-first-traffic-lights-in-westminster-looked-like |website=The Londonist}}</ref> Since then, electricity and computerised control has advanced traffic light technology and increased intersection capacity.<ref name="Sessions" />{{Rp|page=141}}[[File:Trafiksignal Tegelbacken 1953.jpg|thumb|A traffic light in [[Stockholm]], 1953]]

'''Phoenician–Punic literature''' is literature written in [[Phoenician language|Phoenician]], the language of the ancient civilization of [[Phoenicia]], or in the [[Punic language]] that developed from Phoenician and was used in [[Ancient Carthage]]. Its nature and extent are extremely uncertain because there is very little direct evidence. Phoenician and Punic text survives only in inscriptions, of which very few can be interpreted as literary;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barton |first=George A |year=1901 |title=On the Pantheon of Tyre |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/592422 |journal=Journal of the American Oriental Society |volume=22 |issue=22 |pages=115–117 |doi=10.2307/592422 |jstor=592422 |access-date=5 April 2012|url-access=subscription }}{{Blockquote|text=The comparatively few inscriptions which have been brought to light in recent years, consisting as they do of votive and temple inscriptions and grave stones, can hardly be dignified with the name of literature.}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Krahmalkov |first=Charles R. |url=https://archive.org/details/charles-r.-krahmalkov-a-phoenician-punic-grammar/mode/2up |title=A Phoenician-Punic Grammar |publisher=Brill |year=2001 |location=Leiden; Boston; Köln |pages=13–15}}</ref> on coins; and via Greek and Latin sources, such as the fragments of [[Sanchuniathon]]'s ''History'' and [[Mago (agricultural writer)|Mago]]'s agricultural treatise, the Greek translation of the voyage of [[Hanno the Navigator]], and a few lines in the ''[[Poenulus]]'' by [[Plautus]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Amor Ruibal |first=Ángel María |year=2005 |title=Los problemas fundamentales de la filología comparada: su historía, su naturaleza y sus diversas relaciones científicas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8iFy9nGX2uEC&dq=%22literatura+fenicia%22&pg=PA496 |publisher=Consello da Cultura Galega |page=496 |language=Spanish |isbn=8496530078 |access-date=2022-06-11 |archive-date=2015-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150408092251/http://books.google.es/books?id=8iFy9nGX2uEC&pg=PA496&lpg=PA496&dq=%22literatura%20fenicia%22&source=bl&ots=Z_E7Faj79F&sig=FnzbXNVo8eckoW1dZiSGsvvmjqQ&hl=ca&ei=_Q4STrWRKM3GtAaP6rj2Dg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=3&ved=0CC0Q6AEwAjgK#v=onepage&q=%22literatura%20fenicia%22&f=true |url-status=live }}</ref>

This limited evidence has led some scholars to argue that there was not a substantial literary tradition in Phoenician or Punic.<ref name=":7" /> However, Greek and Roman writings suggest that both Phoenicia and Carthage had extensive libraries and produced literature, including the Phoenician sources used by Greek and Latin writers like [[Philo of Byblos]] and [[Menander of Ephesus]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Martín Ruiz |first=Juan Antonio |year=2007 |title=Los libros púnicos de Cartago: a la búsqueda de un saber perdido |url=http://independent.academia.edu/JuanAntonioMart%C3%ADnRuiz/Papers/1276014/Los_libros_punicos_de_Cartago_a_la_busqueda_de_un_saber_perdido |journal=Byrsa: Revista semestrale di arte, cultura e archeologia del mediterraneo punico |language=Spanish |publisher=Polis expresse |volume=VI |issue=1–2 |access-date=2022-06-11 |archive-date=2019-09-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190912042419/https://www.academia.edu/1207733/Los_libros_p%C3%BAnicos_de_Cartago_a_la_b%C3%BAsqueda_de_un_saber_perdido |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Encyclopédie Larousse |year=2002 |title=littérature phénicienne |url=http://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/litterature/ph%C3%A9nicienne/176028# |access-date=3 May 2012 |website=Dictionnaire mondial des littératures |language=French |archive-date=4 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004220129/http://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/litterature/ph%C3%A9nicienne/176028 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Zinc_finger_rendered.png|alt=A twisted band, with one side painted blue and another gray. Its two ends are connected through some chemical species to a green atom (zinc).|thumb|[[Zinc fingers]] help read DNA sequences.]]
[[Zinc]] is an essential element for all known forms of life.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Zinc is a metal essential to life|author1=Andy Weiss|author2=Caitlin Murdoch|date=25 May 2022|journal=ASBMB Today|publisher=[[American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology]]|url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmb-today/science/052522/zinc-is-a-metal-essential-to-life}}</ref> In humans, zinc is required for the function of over 300 [[Enzyme|enzymes]] and 1000 [[Transcription factor|transcription factors]],<ref name="Zinc & sleep 2017 review" /> and is stored and transferred in [[Metallothionein|metallothioneins]].<ref name="Cotton1999bio">{{harvnb|Cotton et al.|1999|pp=625–629}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Plum LM, Rink L, Haase H | title = The essential toxin: impact of zinc on human health | journal = International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | volume = 7 | issue = 4 | pages = 1342–1365 | date = April 2010 | pmid = 20617034 | pmc = 2872358 | doi = 10.3390/ijerph7041342 | doi-access = free }}</ref> It is the second most abundant trace metal in humans after [[Iron in biology|iron]]. It is the only metal which appears in all [[Enzyme#Naming conventions|enzyme classes]].<ref name="Broadley2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Broadley MR, White PJ, Hammond JP, Zelko I, Lux A | title = Zinc in plants | journal = The New Phytologist | volume = 173 | issue = 4 | pages = 677–702 | date = 2007 | pmid = 17286818 | doi = 10.1111/j.1469-8137.2007.01996.x | doi-access =  | bibcode = 2007NewPh.173..677B }}</ref><ref name="Zinc & sleep 2017 review">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cherasse Y, Urade Y | title = Dietary Zinc Acts as a Sleep Modulator | journal = International Journal of Molecular Sciences | volume = 18 | issue = 11 | page = 2334 | date = November 2017 | pmid = 29113075 | pmc = 5713303 | doi = 10.3390/ijms18112334 | quote = Zinc is the second most abundant trace metal in the human body, and is essential for many biological processes.  ... The trace metal zinc is an essential cofactor for more than 300 enzymes and 1000 transcription factors [16]. ... In the central nervous system, zinc is the second most abundant trace metal and is involved in many processes. In addition to its role in enzymatic activity, it also plays a major role in cell signaling and modulation of neuronal activity. | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In proteins, zinc [[ions]] are often coordinated to the [[amino acid]] [[Side chain|side chains]] of [[aspartic acid]], [[glutamic acid]], [[cysteine]] and [[histidine]]. The theoretical and computational description of this zinc binding in proteins (as well as that of other [[transition metal]]s) is difficult.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brandt EG, Hellgren M, Brinck T, Bergman T, Edholm O | title = Molecular dynamics study of zinc binding to cysteines in a peptide mimic of the alcohol dehydrogenase structural zinc site | journal = Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics | volume = 11 | issue = 6 | pages = 975–983 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19177216 | doi = 10.1039/b815482a | url = https://zenodo.org/record/996012 | access-date = 2022-07-02 | url-status = live | bibcode = 2009PCCP...11..975B | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210518085048/https://zenodo.org/record/996012 | archive-date = 2021-05-18 }}</ref>

Roughly {{nowrap|2–4}} grams of zinc<ref name="Rink2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Rink L, Gabriel P | title = Zinc and the immune system | journal = The Proceedings of the Nutrition Society | volume = 59 | issue = 4 | pages = 541–552 | date = November 2000 | pmid = 11115789 | doi = 10.1017/S0029665100000781 | doi-access = free }}</ref> are distributed throughout the human body. Most zinc is in the brain, muscle, bones, kidney, and liver, with the highest concentrations in the prostate and parts of the eye.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Wapnir RA |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qfKdaCoZS18C |title=Protein Nutrition and Mineral Absorption |date=1990 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-8493-5227-0 |location=Boca Raton, Florida |access-date=2022-07-02 |archive-date=2022-04-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220425145646/https://books.google.com/books?id=qfKdaCoZS18C |url-status=live }}</ref><!--page 131--> [[Semen]] contains a particularly high amount of  zinc, a key factor in [[prostate gland]] function and [[reproductive organ]] growth.<ref name="Berdanier2007">{{cite book | vauthors = Berdanier CD, Dwyer JT, Feldman EB |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PJpieIePsmUC |title=Handbook of Nutrition and Food |date=2007 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-8493-9218-4 |location=Boca Raton, Florida |access-date=2022-07-02 |archive-date=2021-04-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210413152707/https://books.google.com/books?id=PJpieIePsmUC |url-status=live }}</ref><!--page 210-->

Zinc homeostasis of the body is mainly controlled by the intestine. Here, [[SLC39A4|ZIP4]] and especially [[TRPM7]] were linked to intestinal zinc uptake essential for postnatal survival.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mittermeier L, Demirkhanyan L, Stadlbauer B, Breit A, Recordati C, Hilgendorff A, Matsushita M, Braun A, Simmons DG, Zakharian E, Gudermann T, Chubanov V | display-authors = 6 | title = TRPM7 is the central gatekeeper of intestinal mineral absorption essential for postnatal survival | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 116 | issue = 10 | pages = 4706–4715 | date = March 2019 | pmid = 30770447 | pmc = 6410795 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1810633116 | bibcode = 2019PNAS..116.4706M | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kasana S, Din J, Maret W | title = Genetic causes and gene–nutrient interactions in mammalian zinc deficiencies: acrodermatitis enteropathica and transient neonatal zinc deficiency as examples | journal = Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology | volume = 29 | pages = 47–62 | date = January 2015 | pmid = 25468189 | doi = 10.1016/j.jtemb.2014.10.003 | bibcode = 2015JTEMB..29...47K }}</ref>

In humans, the biological roles of zinc are ubiquitous.<ref name="Hambridge2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hambidge KM, Krebs NF | title = Zinc deficiency: a special challenge | journal = The Journal of Nutrition | volume = 137 | issue = 4 | pages = 1101–1105 | date = April 2007 | pmid = 17374687 | doi = 10.1093/jn/137.4.1101 | name-list-style = amp | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Zinc - brain disorders 2015 review">{{cite journal | vauthors = Prakash A, Bharti K, Majeed AB | title = Zinc: indications in brain disorders | journal = Fundamental & Clinical Pharmacology | volume = 29 | issue = 2 | pages = 131–149 | date = April 2015 | pmid = 25659970 | doi = 10.1111/fcp.12110 | s2cid = 21141511 }}</ref> It interacts with "a wide range of organic [[Ligand|ligands]]",<ref name="Hambridge2007" /> and has roles in the metabolism of RNA and DNA, [[signal transduction]], and [[gene expression]]. It also regulates [[apoptosis]]. A review from 2015 indicated that about 10% of human proteins (~3000) bind zinc,<ref name="pmid26055706">{{cite journal | vauthors = Djoko KY, Ong CL, Walker MJ, McEwan AG | title = The Role of Copper and Zinc Toxicity in Innate Immune Defense against Bacterial Pathogens | journal = The Journal of Biological Chemistry | volume = 290 | issue = 31 | pages = 18954–18961 | date = July 2015 | pmid = 26055706 | pmc = 4521016 | doi = 10.1074/jbc.R115.647099 | quote = Zn is present in up to 10% of proteins in the human proteome and computational analysis predicted that ~30% of these ~3000 Zn-containing proteins are crucial cellular enzymes, such as hydrolases, ligases, transferases, oxidoreductases, and isomerases (42,43). | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2015JBiCh.29018954D }}</ref> in addition to hundreds more that transport and traffic zinc; a similar ''[[in silico]]'' study in the plant ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' found 2367 zinc-related proteins.<ref name="Broadley2007" />

In the [[brain]], zinc is stored in specific [[synaptic vesicles]] by [[glutamatergic]] [[Neuron|neurons]] and can modulate [[neuronal excitability]].<ref name="Zinc - brain disorders 2015 review" /><ref name="Bitanihirwe">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bitanihirwe BK, Cunningham MG | title = Zinc: the brain's dark horse | journal = Synapse | volume = 63 | issue = 11 | pages = 1029–1049 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 19623531 | doi = 10.1002/syn.20683 | s2cid = 206520330 }}</ref><ref name="Zinc & sleep 2017 review" /> It plays a key role in [[synaptic plasticity]] and so in learning.<ref name="Zinc - brain disorders 2015 review" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nakashima AS, Dyck RH | title = Zinc and cortical plasticity | journal = Brain Research Reviews | volume = 59 | issue = 2 | pages = 347–373 | date = March 2009 | pmid = 19026685 | doi = 10.1016/j.brainresrev.2008.10.003 | s2cid = 22507338 }}</ref> Zinc [[homeostasis]] also plays a critical role in the functional regulation of the [[central nervous system]].<ref name="Zinc - brain disorders 2015 review" /><ref name="Bitanihirwe" /><ref name="Zinc & sleep 2017 review" /> Dysregulation of zinc homeostasis in the central nervous system that results in excessive synaptic zinc concentrations is believed to induce [[neurotoxicity]] through mitochondrial oxidative stress (e.g., by disrupting certain enzymes involved in the [[electron transport chain]], including [[complex I]], [[complex III]], and [[α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase]]), the dysregulation of calcium homeostasis, glutamatergic neuronal [[excitotoxicity]], and interference with intraneuronal [[signal transduction]].<ref name="Zinc - brain disorders 2015 review" /><ref name="pmid25265815">{{cite journal | vauthors = Tyszka-Czochara M, Grzywacz A, Gdula-Argasińska J, Librowski T, Wiliński B, Opoka W | title = The role of zinc in the pathogenesis and treatment of central nervous system (CNS) diseases. Implications of zinc homeostasis for proper CNS function | journal = Acta Poloniae Pharmaceutica | volume = 71 | issue = 3 | pages = 369–377 | date = May 2014 | pmid = 25265815 | url = http://www.ptfarm.pl/pub/File/Acta_Poloniae/2014/3/369.pdf | url-status = live | df = mdy-all | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170829234531/http://www.ptfarm.pl/pub/File/Acta_Poloniae/2014/3/369.pdf | archive-date = August 29, 2017 }}</ref> L- and D-histidine facilitate brain zinc uptake.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yokel RA | title = Blood-brain barrier flux of aluminum, manganese, iron and other metals suspected to contribute to metal-induced neurodegeneration | journal = Journal of Alzheimer's Disease | volume = 10 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 223–253 | date = November 2006 | pmid = 17119290 | doi = 10.3233/JAD-2006-102-309 }}</ref> 

[[SLC30A3]] is the primary [[Solute carrier family#Solute carrier family 30|zinc transporter]] involved in cerebral zinc homeostasis.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SLC30A3 solute carrier family 30 member 3 [Homo sapiens (human)] - Gene - NCBI |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/7781 |access-date=2026-08-07 |website=www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov}}</ref>
